questions.q: What did the Teacher discover about pleasure?
questions.a: The Teacher discovered that pleasure was also only temporary.

questions.q: What did the Teacher say about laughter?
questions.a: The Teacher said that laughter was madness and that pleasure accomplished nothing good.

questions.q: What did the Teacher want to find out?
questions.a: The Teacher wanted to find out what was good for people to do during the days of their lives.

questions.q: What did the Teacher build for himself?
questions.a: The Teacher built houses and planted vineyards for himself.

questions.q: What did the Teacher plant in his orchards and parks?
questions.a: He planted a tree of every kind of fruit in them.

questions.q: Why did the Teacher create pools of water?
questions.a: The Teacher created pools of water to water a forest of growing trees.

questions.q: What did the Teacher own more of than anyone else in Jerusalem?
questions.a: He owned more cattle and sheep than anyone who had lived in Jerusalem before him.

questions.q: How did the Teacher find personal pleasure?
questions.a: The Teacher took many wives and concubines to give himself pleasure.

questions.q: What did the Teacher have more of than anyone before him in Jerusalem?
questions.a: He had more wealth, power, and honor than anyone who had lived in Jerusalem before him, and his wisdom remained with him.

questions.q: In what did the Teacher’s heart rejoice?
questions.a: The Teacher’s heart rejoiced in all his hard work.

questions.q: Where was there no profit?
questions.a: There was no profit in any of his labors on the earth.

questions.q: What did the Teacher turn to consider?
questions.a: The Teacher turned to consider wisdom, madness, and folly.

questions.q: What did the Teacher say is more profitable than folly?
questions.a: The Teacher said that wisdom is more profitable than folly, just as light is better than darkness.

questions.q: What did the Teacher realize would happen to him just as it happens to the fool?
questions.a: The Teacher realized that the same fate, death, would happen to him just as it happens to the fool.

questions.q: Who is not remembered for very long?
questions.a: The wise person, like the fool, is not remembered for very long.

questions.q: What did the Teacher say he hated?
questions.a: The Teacher said he hated life because the work done under the sun seemed temporary and insubstantial to him.

questions.q: Why did the Teacher hate all his accomplishments?
questions.a: The Teacher hated all his accomplishments because he would have to leave them to the person who came after him.

questions.q: What did the Teacher say no one knows about the person who will come after him?
questions.a: The Teacher said no one knows whether that person will be wise or foolish.

questions.q: How did the Teacher’s heart feel about his work?
questions.a: The Teacher’s heart began to despair over all the work that he did.

questions.q: What happens to what a wise, skillful person has worked for?
questions.a: He must leave it to someone who did not work for it.

questions.q: What does the Teacher ask about all of a person’s hard work?
questions.a: He asks what lasting benefit a person gets from all his hard work.

questions.q: Why does the hard worker’s heart not find rest at night?
questions.a: Every day his work causes him pain and stress, so at night his heart does not rest.

questions.q: What does the Teacher conclude is the best that people can do?
questions.a: There is nothing better for anyone than to simply eat and drink and be satisfied with what is good in his work.

questions.q: According to the Teacher, who can eat and enjoy life apart from God?
questions.a: No one can eat and enjoy life apart from God.

questions.q: What does God give to the sinner?
questions.a: To the sinner, God gives the work of gathering and collecting wealth, which God then gives to someone who pleases him.

commentary.text: The vanity and vexation of mirth, sensual pleasure, riches, and pomp. (Eccl. 2:1-11) Human wisdom insufficient. (Eccl. 2:12-17) This world to be used according to the will of God. (Eccl. 2:18-26)

Eccl. 2:1-11 Solomon soon found mirth and pleasure to be vanity. What does noisy, flashy mirth towards making a man happy? The manifold devices of men's hearts, to get satisfaction from the world, and their changing from one thing to another, are like the restlessness of a man in a fever. Perceiving it was folly to give himself to wine, he next tried the costly amusements of princes. The poor, when they read such a description, are ready to feel discontent. But the remedy against all such feelings is in the estimate of it all by the owner himself. All was vanity and vexation of spirit: and the same things would yield the same result to us, as to Solomon. Having food and raiment, let us therewith be content. His wisdom remained with him; a strong understanding, with great human knowledge. But every earthly pleasure, when unconnected with better blessings, leaves the mind as eager and unsatisfied as before. Happiness arises not from the situation in which we are placed. It is only through Jesus Christ that final blessedness can be attained.

Eccl. 2:12-17 Solomon found that knowledge and prudence were preferable to ignorance and folly, though human wisdom and knowledge will not make a man happy. The most learned of men, who dies a stranger to Christ Jesus, will perish equally with the most ignorant; and what good can commendations on earth do to the body in the grave, or the soul in hell? And the spirits of just men made perfect cannot want them. So that if this were all, we might be led to hate our life, as it is all vanity and vexation of spirit.

Eccl. 2:18-26 Our hearts are very loth to quit their expectations of great things from the creature; but Solomon came to this at length. The world is a vale of tears, even to those that have much of it. See what fools they are, who make themselves drudges to the world, which affords a man nothing better than subsistence for the body. And the utmost he can attain in this respect is to allow himself a sober, cheerful use thereof, according to his rank and condition. But we must enjoy good in our labour; we must use those things to make us diligent and cheerful in worldly business. And this is the gift of God. Riches are a blessing or a curse to a man, according as he has, or has not, a heart to make a good use of them. To those that are accepted of the Lord, he gives joy and satisfaction in the knowledge and love of him. But to the sinner he allots labour, sorrow, vanity, and vexation, in seeking a worldly portion, which yet afterwards comes into better hands. Let the sinner seriously consider his latter end. To seek a lasting portion in the love of Christ and the blessings it bestows, is the only way to true and satisfying enjoyment even of this present world.
